history.hpi: Parents report the infant has had a fever since yesterday, progressively more difficult to console today, and has refused her bottle for several hours. This evening she became unusually sleepy and hard to arouse, prompting the 911 call. No vomiting or diarrhea reported. No known sick contacts, though an older sibling attends daycare.
history.lastOralIntake: Refused bottle for approximately 5 hours prior to EMS arrival
history.events: Fever and decreased activity over the day; parents called 911 when the infant became difficult to arouse and felt warm and clammy

scene.location: Second-floor apartment, living room, infant held in mother's arms
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; apartment cluttered but passable
scene.bystanders: Both parents present, visibly anxious; older sibling (4 years old) also in the home
visualCues: Infant lethargic and limp in mother's arms
Mottled, dusky skin on the extremities
No rash noted on exposed skin
Diaper appears dry, mother reports no wet diapers in over 6 hours

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 6-month-old female who is lethargic, febrile, and difficult to arouse. She has mottled skin, delayed capillary refill, and a sunken fontanelle consistent with poor perfusion and dehydration.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, weak high-pitched cry with stimulation
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, mild subcostal retractions, no stridor or wheeze
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak, thready peripheral pulses; delayed capillary refill approximately 4 seconds
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Weak spontaneous movement of all extremities, poor muscle tone
otherFindings: Mother reports no wet diaper in over 6 hours
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Weak, high-pitched cry with stimulation; minimal spontaneous movement

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes signs of septic shock (tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, sunken fontanelle, fever, decreased mental status) and attempts vascular access; given poor peripheral perfusion in a hypoperfused infant, an IO needle is placed and isotonic fluid boluses are initiated per pediatric shock dosing.

phases.name: IO access obtained, fluids started
phases.description: Crew places an IO line after anticipating difficult peripheral access in this hypoperfused infant, checks blood glucose, and begins a weight-based isotonic fluid bolus toward pediatric shock resuscitation targets.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing shock physiology, the crew places an IO line rather than attempting prolonged peripheral IV access in a hypoperfused infant, then begins 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses toward pediatric shock targets while checking blood glucose and providing advance hospital notification.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak peripheral pulses, capillary refill improving slightly to 3 seconds
otherFindings: IO needle secured in proximal tibia
Blood glucose 90 mg/dL, no correction needed
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Weak cry, slightly more responsive to voice

expectedActions.shortAction: Place IO needle for vascular access given anticipated difficult peripheral IV in a hypoperfused infant
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Rapid vascular access is essential in decompensating pediatric shock; peripheral IV attempts are often futile in a severely hypoperfused infant.

expectedActions.shortAction: Normal saline bolus 150 mL IV/IO (7.5 kg x 20 mL/kg = 150 mL) over less than 15 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pediatric Fluid goal of up to a total of 60 mL/kg or 1 liter of isotonic fluid by giving 20 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid boluses (for cardiogenic shock give 10 mL/kg boluses)
expectedActions.rationale: Early aggressive fluid resuscitation is essential for suspected pediatric septic shock.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose; correct with dextrose if less than 60 mg/dL
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood sugar, and correct if less than 60 mg/dL
expectedActions.rationale: Hypoglycemia is common in septic infants and can mimic or worsen altered mental status.

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide advance notification to receiving hospital for suspected pediatric septic shock
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide advanced notification to the hospital
expectedActions.rationale: Advance notice allows the receiving pediatric team to prepare for rapid sepsis management on arrival.

transitions.condition: After the first 20 mL/kg bolus, reassessment shows persistent tachycardia and delayed capillary refill, so a second 20 mL/kg bolus is administered toward the up-to-60 mL/kg goal; mental status and perfusion begin to improve.

Vascular access is delayed or fluid boluses are withheld despite clear signs of compensated septic shock; the infant progresses toward uncompensated shock as tachycardia worsens and systolic blood pressure falls toward the pediatric hypotension threshold.

phases.name: Repeat bolus given, perfusion improves
phases.description: After a second weight-based fluid bolus, the infant shows improving perfusion with decreasing heart rate, improving capillary refill, and better responsiveness. The crew continues serial reassessment en route to the hospital.
phases.triggerCondition: After the first 20 mL/kg bolus, reassessment shows persistent tachycardia and delayed capillary refill, so a second 20 mL/kg bolus is administered toward the up-to-60 mL/kg goal; mental status and perfusion begin to improve.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Peripheral pulses stronger, capillary refill improved to under 2 seconds
otherFindings: Second 150 mL bolus completed (300 mL total, toward 450 mL/60 mL/kg goal)
Mother reports infant appears more like herself

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat normal saline bolus 150 mL IV/IO (7.5 kg x 20 mL/kg = 150 mL), total 300 mL toward 450 mL (60 mL/kg) goal
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pediatric Fluid goal of up to a total of 60 mL/kg or 1 liter of isotonic fluid by giving 20 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid boluses
expectedActions.rationale: Persistent tachycardia and delayed capillary refill after the first bolus indicate ongoing hypoperfusion requiring additional fluid toward the total goal.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs, perfusion, and mental status after each fluid bolus
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Full vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) with reassessment q 15 minutes or more frequently as appropriate
expectedActions.rationale: Frequent reassessment identifies whether the infant is responding to fluids or trending toward cardiogenic shock, which would require withholding further boluses.

phases.name: IO access delayed, fluids withheld
phases.description: Vascular access and fluid resuscitation are delayed despite clear signs of compensated septic shock. The infant decompensates, with worsening tachycardia, dropping blood pressure below the pediatric hypotension threshold, and declining mental status.
phases.triggerCondition: Vascular access is delayed or fluid boluses are withheld despite clear signs of compensated septic shock; the infant progresses toward uncompensated shock as tachycardia worsens and systolic blood pressure falls toward the pediatric hypotension threshold.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Barely palpable peripheral pulses, capillary refill 5 seconds
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Weak whimper only with painful stimulus

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize uncompensated shock (SBP below 60 mmHg for age); establish IO access emergently and begin fluid bolus
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hypotension for age (lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure in mmHg): Less than 1 years of age: 60. Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Hypotension is a late and ominous sign in pediatric shock; delay beyond this point risks rapid progression to cardiopulmonary failure.
